items.bold: TRUMP CANCELS THE WEEKEND STRIKES — TALKS RESUME TODAY
items.text: Late Saturday, Trump announced on Truth Social that Iran and 'other Middle Eastern countries' had asked the US to hold off on the strikes planned for the weekend, saying 'the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to.' He said he'd agreed to cancel the attack 'for the future benefit of the WORLD' — subject to a deal being rapidly finalized — and that Israel is part of the commitment to hold off. Sunday, Trump confirmed US-Iran negotiations resume today (Monday), telling reporters 'it begins tomorrow afternoon [US time]. We'll see.'

items.bold: SAUDI ARABIA'S MBS PERSONALLY DROVE THE DECISION
items.text: Saudi state media confirmed Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump directly to urge 'de-escalation and diplomacy' and 'prioritizing dialogue to reduce escalation.' A CNN military analyst noted Saudi Arabia is economically exposed — much of its oil and export trade depends on Hormuz reopening — giving Riyadh real leverage with Washington. Reports also point to practical US constraints behind the decision: concerns about depleting Patriot missile stockpiles, the risk of the war becoming a full regional conflagration, and Gulf allies' vulnerability to Iranian retaliation.

Trump says any deal must include the 'Immediate, Complete, and Total Opening' of the Strait of Hormuz and 'an end to Iran's nuclear threat.' A regional official briefed on the mediation told CBS the proposal also calls for Iran to halt attacks by Iraqi militias on Gulf states and Jordan, in exchange for the US ending its naval blockade on Iran and allowing Tehran to resume oil exports under the terms of the earlier, collapsed ceasefire deal. Nothing is signed — Investing.com reports Iran has not yet formally agreed to reopen the strait.

DAY 109-111 — MAJOR CORRECTION: THE MOU WAS SIGNED 2 DAYS EARLY, AT VERSAILLES, NOT BURGENSTOCK. Wednesday June 17 evening: President Trump PERSONALLY SIGNED the US-Iran memorandum of understanding during a state dinner at the Palace of Versailles, France (G7 sidelines), with French President Macron standing beside him. IRAN'S PRESIDENT MASOUD PEZESHKIAN also signed in person — distinct from the earlier digital signing Sunday Jun 15 by VP Vance and Parliament Speaker Qalibaf. PAKISTAN PM SHEHBAZ SHARIF confirmed: 'Islamabad MoU shall enter into force with immediate effect and, as a first step, the Islamic Republic of Iran will instantly reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and the United States of America will immediately lift the naval blockade.' Sharif praised both Khamenei and Pezeshkian for 'wisdom, foresight and statesmanship.' THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION REVEALED THE 14-POINT MOU IN FULL Wednesday: (1) Immediate/permanent end to war on all fronts including Lebanon. (2) Mutual sovereignty respect, non-interference. (3) Hormuz: Iran's lead negotiator Ghalibaf said the strait 'will NOT return to pre-war conditions' — Iran will 'receive a fee for services' to shipping, meaning the PGSA toll framework persists in modified form. (4) Nuclear: Iran 'reaffirms it shall not procure or develop nuclear weapons'; enriched uranium to be 'down-blended on site under the supervision of the IAEA' via a mechanism still to be 'mutually agreed.' (5) $300 BILLION FUND DENIED: Trump — 'not investing 10 cents' — the deal instead permits THIRD-PARTY investment into Iran contingent on compliance, not a direct US fund (refuting earlier FT/Iranian-media reports). KHAMENEI AUTHORISED THE DEAL THURSDAY despite holding 'a different view,' after assurances from Pezeshkian that Iran's rights and 'Resistance Front' interests would be protected; Pezeshkian/SNSC pledged not to yield to 'excessive' future US demands. US LAWMAKERS (both parties) flagged concerns: nuclear verification mechanism undefined, Iran's missile programme not addressed. Trump will send the deal to Congress. IAEA DIRECTOR GROSSI: 'It is good that the memorandum is there. Now the technical work starts.' BURGENSTOCK TODAY (FRIDAY JUN 19): NOT a signing ceremony — Al Jazeera confirms documents 'already signed,' today is 'the official kickoff of the 59 days remaining for these sides to come to a conclusion.' Venue: Burgenstock Resort, Stansstad, near Lucerne, owned by Qatar's Katara Hospitality (same 2024 Ukraine peace summit venue). Vance + Ghalibaf attending. BRENT FRIDAY: $78.31 (-1.6%). assessment.body:
Monday 8:45 AM IST. Day 156. The most hopeful 72 hours of this war so far.

WHAT HAPPENED OVER THE WEEKEND
• Saturday night, Trump announced on Truth Social that Iran and 'other Middle Eastern countries' asked the US to hold off on strikes planned for the weekend, citing 'the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to.' He said the US remains 'locked and loaded' but agreed to cancel the attack 'for the future benefit of the WORLD' — conditional on rapidly finalizing a deal. Israel is reportedly part of the commitment to hold off.
• Sunday, Saudi state media confirmed Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump directly to urge 'de-escalation and diplomacy.' A CNN analyst noted Saudi Arabia is economically exposed via Hormuz and carries real weight with Washington as a key Gulf ally.
• Trump confirmed Sunday that US-Iran negotiations resume today: 'It begins this afternoon. We'll see.'

THE REPORTED DEAL FRAMEWORK
• Trump's stated terms: 'Immediate, Complete, and Total Opening of the Strait of Hormuz, and an end to Iran's nuclear threat.'
• A regional official briefed on mediation told CBS the proposal also includes Iran halting Iraqi-militia attacks on Gulf states and Jordan, in exchange for the US ending its naval blockade on Iran and allowing Tehran to resume oil exports — largely mirroring the terms of the ceasefire deal that collapsed weeks ago.
• Important caveat: Investing.com reports Iran has not formally agreed to reopen the strait. This is a strike pause and a resumed negotiating track — not a signed agreement.

WHY NOW? PRACTICAL FACTORS, NOT JUST DIPLOMACY
• Reporting (NYT, Seoul Economic Daily) suggests the decision reflects real operational constraints as much as diplomatic breakthrough: concerns about depleting US Patriot missile stockpiles, the risk of the conflict spiraling into a full regional war, and the exposure of Gulf allies like Saudi Arabia to Iranian retaliation.

INDIA — THE AUG 1 FUEL REVIEW LANDED SOFTLY
• Despite Brent's 24% July surge (its strongest monthly gain since March), India's August 1 monthly fuel review left domestic LPG, petrol and diesel prices unchanged — only commercial LPG cylinders were cut (₹202 in Delhi, ₹209 in Kolkata for 19kg). The government appears to be absorbing costs via OMCs rather than passing them to households, at least for now.
• The Modi government separately approved 'Samudra Manthan', a ₹84,084 crore national offshore exploration scheme explicitly aimed at reducing India's long-term dependence on oil and gas transiting Hormuz — a strategic, not just tactical, response to this war.

MARKETS
• Brent slipped roughly 5% on the strike-cancellation news, pulling back from Friday's ~$88 close. Gift Nifty is up 136 points to 24,589, pointing to a strong Monday open on the de-escalation hopes.

WATCHLIST
• Whether today's resumed talks produce an actual signed framework, or stall like the June MOU did.
• Whether Iran formally commits to reopening Hormuz — the one concrete deliverable markets are watching for.
• Whether the ceasefire-in-strikes holds through the negotiation, or breaks down as it did after the last pause.

brief: Day 156 of the West Asia war, 8:45 AM update. Overall risk to India right now: easing, cautiously — this is the most hopeful moment of the war so far.

Big news over the weekend: Trump called off planned strikes on Iran after Iran itself, plus Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Qatar, all asked him to hold off — saying the outline of a deal had been agreed. Saudi Arabia's crown prince personally called Trump to push for de-escalation. Talks between the US and Iran restart today.

The deal being discussed would fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end Iran's nuclear threat, in exchange for the US lifting its naval blockade on Iran. Nothing is signed yet, and Iran hasn't formally agreed to reopen the strait — so treat this as a real opening, not a done deal.

Good news for households: even though oil jumped 24% in July — its biggest monthly rise since March — India's August 1 price review left petrol, diesel and home LPG cylinders unchanged. Only commercial LPG got cheaper. The government also approved a big new domestic oil exploration plan to reduce reliance on the strait long-term.

Markets are cheering: oil eased about 5% this morning and Indian futures point to a strong open. Bottom line: after months of escalation, this is the first weekend where the story was genuinely about peace talks resuming rather than new strikes. Worth watching closely whether it holds.
